On such occasions poor Mr. Woodhouse found his feelings in a melancholy conflict. He liked the cloth to be laid, for it had been the fashion of his youth, yet his conviction that heavy suppers were very unwholesome made him rather uneasy at seeing anything placed upon it; and while his hospitality would have welcomed his visitors to everything, his concern for their health caused him sorrow at the thought of them eating.

A small basin of thin gruel, like his own, was all he could, with thorough self‑approval, recommend; though he might restrain himself, while the ladies were comfortably clearing away the finer dishes, to say:

“Mrs. Bates, may I suggest you try one of these eggs? A very soft‑boiled egg is not unwholesome. Serle knows how to boil an egg better than anyone. I would not recommend an egg boiled by anyone else; but you need not be frightened, they are very small, you see—one of our little eggs will not hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma give you a _little_ bit of tart—a _very_ little bit. Ours are all apple‑tarts. You need not fear unwholesome preserves here. I do not advise the custard. Mrs. Goddard, what say you to _half_ a glass of wine? A _small_ half‑glass, diluted with water? I do not think it could disagree with you.”

Emma permitted her father to speak—but she served her guests in a far more satisfactory manner, and on that particular evening took particular pleasure in seeing them depart contented. The happiness of Miss Smith matched her intentions exactly. Miss Woodhouse was such a great figure in Highbury that the prospect of the introduction had brought both anxiety and delight; yet the modest, grateful little girl left with a highly gratified spirit, delighted by the kindness with which Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and at last even shook her hand!

I thought he might appreciate a surprise breakfast, so I slipped forward quietly and tapped his shoulder. He leapt up at once, and it was not the same figure I had seen before, but another.

Yet this second man wore the same coarse grey, bore a great iron on his leg, was lame, hoarse, shivering, and seemed to embody everything the first man had—except his face was different, and he wore a flat, broad‑brimmed, low‑crowned felt hat. I caught all this in an instant, for I had only a moment to glance: he swore at me, swung a weak, round blow that missed and almost knocked himself down, causing him to stagger, then he fled into the mist, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

“It’s the young man!” I thought, my heart leaping as I recognized him. I might have felt a pain in my liver, too, had I known exactly where it was.

Soon after I reached the Battery, and there stood the right man—hugging himself and limping back and forth as if he had never ceased all night—waiting for me. He was terribly cold, indeed. “Brandy,” I replied.

He was already shoveling mincemeat down his throat in a most curious fashion—more like a man stuffing it away in a frantic hurry than actually eating it—but he paused to take a sip of the liquor. When we judge an author's merit and assign him his place among our literary deities, we may view him through our own perspective and measure him by our own criteria. Yet, in assessing the power evident in his works, we must follow his own intentions, placing his creations beside his own ideal to see what is lacking. Our view of art differs from Mr. Poe's. He holds that art should be the production of Beauty, and perhaps we only disagree on the definition of that term. In evaluating his writings, however, we shall employ his own standard as our guide. The temple of the god of song is open on every side, and there is ample space within for all who bring offerings or seek an oracle.

In his stories, Mr. Poe chooses to display his talent chiefly in that shadowy zone that stretches from the farthest reaches of the plausible into the strange realms of superstition and unreality. He unites, in a striking fashion, two faculties rarely found together: the ability to sway the reader's mind with the intangible shadows of mystery, and a meticulous attention to detail that spares no pin or button. Both arise, in truth, from the dominant quality of his mind, which we have earlier termed analysis. It is this that sets the artist apart. His mind simultaneously looks ahead to the effect he wishes to produce. Having decided which emotions to evoke, he makes every subordinate element march toward that single centre. Even his mystery is mathematically precise to his own intellect. To him, X is a known quantity from the start. In any picture he paints he knows the chemical properties of each colour. No matter how vague his figures may appear, no matter how formless the shadows, to him the outline is as clear as a geometric diagram. For this reason Mr. Poe has no sympathy for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within mystery, is wrapped in it; it colours all his thoughts, tinges his vision, and even the most ordinary things acquire a rainbow fringe. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is a spectator _ab extra_. He analyses, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for to him it is practically that—a mechanism of wheels, cogs, and piston‑rods, all working toward a definite end.

This analytical bent balances his poetic side, and by granting him the patience for minutiae, it lets him cast a marvelous reality into his most unreal fantasies. He paints a monomania with great vigor. He delights in dissecting one of those mental cancers and tracing every subtle branch of its roots. In conjuring images of horror he also achieves a strange success, often delivering, through a dim hint, a terrible doubt that lies at the heart of all terror. He leaves the completion of the picture to imagination, a task to which only she is truly suited.

Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

My principal ambition is to launch a periodical to be titled “The Stylus,” yet it would be of no use to me—once established—if it were not wholly free from a publisher’s control. In other words, I intend to create a journal that will be entirely my own in every respect. To achieve this, I must first secure a list of at least five hundred subscribers; I already have nearly two hundred. I plan, however, to travel South and West among my personal and literary acquaintances—old college mates and West Point friends—and see what can be done. To raise the necessary funds for the initial step, I intend to give a lecture at the Society Library on Thursday, the 3rd of February, and, to avoid any quarrel, my topic will not be literary at all. I have selected a broad subject: “The Universe.”

Having now presented you with the facts of the matter, I leave the remainder to the judgment of your own tact and generosity. With deepest gratitude,

Your ever‑faithful friend,
EDGAR A. POE.

Although these letters are brief and written on a whim, we think they sufficiently demonstrate the very qualities that are denied to Mr. Poe—humility, perseverance, belief in another’s friendship, and the capacity for warm and grateful companionship. He possessed these traits when he was sane, and they are the only aspects we have consistently observed in the five or six years we have known him personally. It is far easier to trust what we have seen and experienced than what we hear from others; consequently we remember him with admiration and respect. The portrayals of him made during his periods of mental instability seem, to us, like portraits painted in sickness of a man we only ever knew in health.

Yet there is another, more moving and far more compelling piece of evidence that genuine goodness existed in Edgar A. Poe. To reveal it we must lift the veil that solemnly covers grief and refinement in poverty; we believe this may be justified if it helps brighten the poet’s memory, even if it does not serve a more immediate purpose for those whose lives were broken by his death.

Our first notice of Mr. Poe’s relocation to this city came via a call from a lady who introduced herself as his mother‑in‑law. She was seeking employment for him and justified her request by mentioning his illness, her daughter’s chronic invalidity, and the circumstances that forced her to intervene. The lady’s countenance, made beautiful and saintly by an evident surrender of her life to hardship and tender sorrow, her gentle, mournful voice pleading the case, her long‑forgotten yet instinctively refined manners, and her appealing yet appreciative reference to her son’s talents and claims, at once revealed the presence of one of those earthly angels that women in distress can become.

It was a hard fate she was overseeing. Mr. Poe wrote with painstaking care, his style elevated far above popular taste, which made it difficult for him to earn a decent living.

It became clear that I had greatly exceeded the limits of my experiment and that the worst of the shock was still to come. No mind can form an adequate picture of the horror of my plight. I gasped convulsively for breath, a shudder like a fit of ague shaking every nerve and muscle, my eyes seemed to pop from their sockets, a horrible nausea overwhelmed me, and at last I fainted.

Assuming that, during my ascent, I would encounter an atmosphere essentially like that at the earth’s surface, I imagined that, by means of M. Grimm’s clever device, I could easily condense enough of it for breathing. This would eliminate the principal obstacle to a lunar voyage. I had indeed spent money and considerable effort adapting the apparatus for this purpose, and I looked forward with confidence to its successful use, provided I could complete the journey within a reasonable time. This brings me back to the question of how fast the travel might be.

“It is true that balloons, in the early stages of their rise from the earth, are known to ascend at a comparatively moderate speed. The lifting power comes entirely from the great lightness of the gas in the balloon compared with the surrounding air; and at first glance it seems unlikely that, as the balloon climbs and enters layers of air whose density falls rapidly, the original speed would increase. Yet I was not aware of any recorded ascent in which the absolute rate of rise decreased; such a decline should have occurred, if only because of gas leakage from poorly constructed balloons varnished with ordinary varnish. It seemed, therefore, that the loss of gas merely offset whatever accelerating force might be present. I now thought that, if in my passage I found the medium I had imagined, and if it proved to be essentially what we call atmospheric air, the degree of rarefaction—no matter how extreme—would make little difference to my ascent. The gas in the balloon would itself become rarified in proportion, allowing enough escape to prevent explosion, yet it would remain lighter than any mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. Meanwhile, the pull of gravity would steadily lessen in proportion to the square of the distance, so with a rapidly increasing velocity I would eventually reach those remote zones where the earth’s attraction is outweighed by the moon’s. With these ideas, I saw no reason to burden myself with more provisions than would suffice for forty days.

With these ideas, I didn’t see any reason to carry more provisions than would last forty days.

"There was, however, another problem that gave me some unease. It has been observed that, in balloon ascents to significant heights, besides the difficulty of breathing, people experience severe discomfort in the head and body, often accompanied by nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms, which become increasingly troublesome the higher they go."

Having decided on this plan, I hesitated little. I assumed that, even far from Earth, the air would be essentially the same as at the surface, and that with Mr. Grimm’s clever device I could compress enough of it for breathing. That would remove the biggest obstacle to a trip to the moon. I had already spent money and a great deal of effort adapting the device for this purpose, and I was confident it would work if I could finish the journey in a reasonable time. This brings me back to the question of how fast the travel might be.

It is true that balloons, when they first rise from the ground, ascend at a fairly modest speed. Their lift comes entirely from the gas inside being lighter than the surrounding air, and at first glance it does not seem likely that the balloon would speed up as it climbs into thinner and thinner layers of atmosphere. Yet I have never seen any recorded ascent where the upward speed actually slowed down, even though one would expect it to, for example because poorly made balloons leak gas through ordinary varnish. It seemed that any loss of gas was just enough to cancel out any accelerating force. I now think that, if I find the medium I imagined on my journey, and if it turns out to be essentially what we call atmospheric air, the exact degree of thinness will not matter much for my ascent. The gas in the balloon will also become thinner, but it will still be lighter than any mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. Meanwhile, Earth’s gravity weakens with the square of the distance, so my speed would increase dramatically, and eventually I would reach a region where the moon’s pull outweighs Earth’s. With these ideas, I decided that I did not need to carry more supplies than would last forty days.

It has been observed that, during balloon climbs to great heights, besides the difficulty of breathing, people feel great discomfort in the head and body, often with nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms that become more severe the higher they go.

This process, repeated many times, eventually filled the chamber with an atmosphere suitable for breathing. Yet, in such a confined space the air would soon become foul and unsuitable for the lungs. "April 5th. Observed the curious spectacle of the sun's ascent while almost the whole visible face of the earth remained shrouded in darkness. In time the light spread over everything, and once more I discerned the line of ice to the north. It now stood very clear, of a darker shade than the ocean's waters. I was evidently drawing nearer, and with great speed. I fancied I could again make out a strip of land to the east, and another to the west, though I could not be certain. Weather moderate. "April 6th. Was astonished to find the ice rim at a very moderate distance, and an immense expanse of the same substance stretching to the horizon in the north. It was clear that, should the balloon maintain its present course, it would soon pass over the Frozen Ocean, and I now had little doubt of eventually seeing the Pole. Throughout the day I continued to approach the ice. Toward evening the limits of my horizon suddenly and markedly expanded, undoubtedly due to the earth's shape as an oblate spheroid, and my ascent above the flattened region near the Arctic Circle. When darkness finally overtook me, I went to bed in great anxiety, fearing that I might cross the object of such curiosity without the chance to observe it.

"April 7th. Rose early, and to my great delight at last beheld what could not be mistaken for anything but the northern Pole itself. This, indeed, is the case. I possess a great—indeed a very great—amount of information which I would take the utmost pleasure in conveying. I have much to report about the planet’s climate; its marvelous swings between heat and cold, the unrelenting, scorching sunshine that lasts a fortnight and then gives way to a chill far beyond polar frost; the continual movement of moisture, distilled as if in a vacuum, from the point directly under the sun to the point farthest from it; the shifting streams of water; the inhabitants themselves; their manners, customs, and political structures; their odd physical make‑up; their ugliness; their lack of ears—those useless appendages in an atmosphere so peculiarly altered; their resulting ignorance of speech’s use and properties; their replacement for speech in a singular mode of inter‑communication; the incomprehensible link between each individual on the moon and a particular individual on Earth—a connection analogous to, and dependent upon, that of the planet’s orbs and its satellites, by which the lives and destinies of one’s inhabitants are intertwined with those of the other; and above all, if it pleases your Excellencies—above all, those dark and hideous mysteries that lie in the moon’s outer regions—areas that, because of the almost miraculous synchrony of the satellite’s rotation on its axis with its sidereal revolution around Earth, have never been turned toward, and, by God’s mercy, never shall be turned toward, the scrutiny of man’s telescopes. All this, and far more—much more—I would gladly detail. Yet, to be concise, I must ask for my reward. I yearn to return to my family and my home; and as the price for any further communication on my part—considering the light I can shed on many crucial branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must, through the influence of your honorable body, request a pardon for the crime I committed in the death of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of the present paper. Its bearer, a moon inhabitant whom I have persuaded and properly instructed to act as my messenger to Earth, will await your Excellencies’ pleasure and return to me with the pardon, if it can in any way be obtained.

“I have the honor to be, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

The mental qualities described as analytical are, in themselves, scarcely amenable to analysis. We perceive them only through their effects. We know, among other things, that when a mind is overly possessed by them they become a source of the keenest pleasure. Just as a strong man revels in his physical power, delighting in exercises that call his muscles to work, so the analyst exults in the moral activity of untangling. He finds enjoyment even in the most trivial tasks that allow his talent to be exercised. He is attracted to riddles, puzzles, hieroglyphs; in each solution he displays a degree of acumen that seems, to ordinary perception, almost supernatural. His conclusions, produced by the very soul and essence of method, in truth possess the whole character of intuition.

The power of re‑solution is perhaps greatly strengthened by mathematical study, especially by that highest branch which, unjustly and merely because of its backward‑looking operations, has been styled, as if par excellence, analysis. Yet calculation is not in itself analysis. A chess‑player, for example, performs one without effort the other. Hence the game of chess, in its influence on mental character, is widely misunderstood. I am not now composing a treatise, but merely prefacing a somewhat singular narrative with observations drawn at random; I will therefore take the opportunity to assert that the higher faculties of reflective intellect are more decisively and more usefully exercised by the modest game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In the latter, where the pieces possess different and bizarre motions, with various and shifting values, what is merely complex is often mistaken (a not uncommon error) for what is profound.
